topic: Modals of deduction in the past (must have done...)

questions.explanation: 'Must have + past participle' deduces a past cause from evidence.

questions.q: She can't have ___ — she was with me.
questions.explanation: 'Can't have + past participle' rules out a past possibility.
'Can't have' expresses impossibility about the past.

options: You must be exhausted after the marathon.
You must have exhaust after the marathon.
You must have been exhausted after the marathon.
You had to be exhausted after the marathon.
questions.explanation: 'Must have been' deduces a past state with certainty.
Evidence against it needs 'can't have + past participle'.
'Must have + past participle' is a certain deduction about the past.

options: They mustn't have finished already — they only started an hour ago.
They couldn't have finish already — they only started an hour ago.
They can't finished already — they only started an hour ago.
They can't have finished already — they only started an hour ago.
questions.explanation: 'Can't have' expresses past impossibility, not 'mustn't have'.
Use 'must have + past participle' for a certain past deduction.

questions.q: She ___ — she was at home all evening.
questions.explanation: An alibi makes it impossible: 'can't have + past participle'.

options: You should tell me — I could have helped.
You should have told me — I could help.
You should have told me — I could have helped.
You should had told me — I could have helped.
questions.explanation: 'Should have' criticises a past omission; 'could have' offers a missed possibility.
'Must have + past participle' deduces what surely happened.

questions.q: He ___ — the door was locked from inside.
questions.explanation: Impossibility about the past needs 'can't have + past participle'.

options: She might miss the bus — that's why she's late.
She might have miss the bus — that's why she's late.
She may have missed the bus — that's why she'll be late.
She might have missed the bus — that's why she's late.
questions.explanation: 'Might have + past participle' suggests a possible past cause.

options: must have left the window open
must have leave the window open
had to leave the window open
questions.explanation: Evidence of a past mistake needs 'must have + past participle'.
A certain past deduction uses 'must have + past participle'.

options: They may have gone to the beach — the car is gone.
They may go to the beach — the car is gone.
They may have go to the beach — the car is gone.
They must have gone to the beach — the car is gone.
questions.explanation: 'May have' keeps the deduction uncertain, unlike 'must have'.
'Might have + past participle' suggests a possible past event.
Evidence against a past action needs 'can't have + past participle'.
'Could have' reproaches someone for a past risk.
'Can't have been' rules out a past state.
